REAGENT 2.0.1 SWALLOWS :on-recoverable-error — hydration error-capture harnesses built on reagent.dom.client/hydrate-root are VACUOUS. Found by the rf2-53lsj worker (#6407) on 2026-07-19, in its OWN test harness, before shipping. Reagent destructures :on-recoverable-error and NEVER PASSES IT to React hydrateRoot, so the callback fires for nothing: the harness captured NOTHING on either input and passed identically on broken and fixed HTML. Driving React hydrateRoot DIRECTLY, React 19 correctly reports the mismatch ("Hydration failed... + revenue / - :revenue").
RULE: to assert on hydration mismatches, call React hydrateRoot directly. Do not route through Reagent for error capture. And whatever harness you use, PROVE IT CAPTURES: feed it known-bad input and confirm it reports, before trusting a green on good input.
SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME PR, easy to get backwards: Reagent renders a keyword/symbol child via (name x), which DROPS THE NAMESPACE — :a/b renders as "b", not "a/b". A JVM emitter fix that merely strips the leading colon would emit "a/b" and leave the hosts FURTHER apart while appearing closer. Namespaced symbols diverge identically. Always diff the actual BYTES against the client, never reason about the shape.

Reagent's get-react-key (reagent2.impl.template L407) only reads :key meta from VECTORS. ^{:key k} attached to a function-call list form (e.g. ^{:key g} (group-section g …)) is lost on evaluation — the meta lives on the source list at READ time, not on the returned value. Two fixes: (a) put ^{:key k} on the vector literal returned by the function, or (b) wrap the result in (with-meta result {:key k}). Found in views_view.cljs PR #1471 fixing rf2-gphsi; same anti-pattern exists across several other panels (audit bead rf2-?? filed). Tell future test authors: a test that asserts :key meta on the rendered child reproduces the bug.

REBASE conflict resolution: --ours/--theirs INVERT vs merge. In a rebase, --ours = the branch you are replaying ONTO (e.g. origin/main), --theirs = the commit being replayed (the worker's own branch). So to take MAIN's version of a generated file (e.g. docs/cljs/playground-rf2.js) during a rebase, use 'git checkout --ours <file>', NOT --theirs. My earlier dispatch instructions said --theirs for this and were WRONG (caught by the rf2-ywwpx worker on #6284, 2026-07-18, which verified empirically: stage2/--ours == origin/main, stage3/--theirs == its own stale commit). Harmless for a generated file that gets regenerated afterwards, but on a NON-generated conflict the same wording silently takes the wrong side and can revert main's work. ALWAYS instruct workers to verify which stage matches origin/main (git show :2:<file> / :3:<file> and compare digests) rather than trusting the label.

Rebase-merge makes a worker branch look UNMERGED to an ancestry check. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` returns N>0 and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` fails for a branch whose PR was merged with --rebase, because the rebase rewrote the SHAs. Judging 'abandoned, holds unmerged work' from that heuristic mislabelled 7 of 9 branches in one hygiene pass (their PRs #7096-#7107 were all merged). The authoritative test is PATCH-ID containment: `git cherry origin/main origin/<branch>` counting '^+' lines == 0 means fully merged. Confirm with `gh pr view --json state` == MERGED as the second signal.

To tell my own checkout-race reverts apart from genuine reviewer reopens I grepped bead notes for "AUDIT-REOPEN|MERGED-PR AUDIT". rf2-zt65l carried a note spelled "AUDIT REOPEN (PR #6921 ...)" — SPACE, not hyphen — so my grep returned 0, I concluded "my race, not a reviewer", and re-closed a bead whose audit finding was still unmet. That is exactly the failure mode I had been guarding against all session, produced by my own detection code. CORRECTED PATTERN, use this: grep -ciE "audit.?reopen|merged-pr audit|reopened|REOPEN" — case-insensitive, tolerant of hyphen/space/underscore, and including bare "REOPENED" which several audits use as the leading verb. BETTER STILL: do not rely on a single grep. Before re-closing ANY bead that reads open after you closed it, READ the recent notes (bd show | tail) with your eyes. A close is destructive to an audit obligation and cheap to defer; when the two hypotheses are "my tooling reverted it" and "a reviewer reopened it with a finding", the cost of being wrong is asymmetric — assume reviewer unless the notes plainly show otherwise. THE UNDERLYING LESSON, which recurs: a negative grep result is weak evidence. It proves your PATTERN did not match, never that the THING is absent. Same class as "grep -c beads <file> || echo NO HOOK" (grep exits 1 on zero count, not only on a missing file) and the "&& / ||" precedence bug that truncated issues.jsonl. ROOT CAUSE (final): BEADS GIT HOOKS AUTO-IMPORT THE JSONL — 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads' DESTROYS CLOSES EVEN WITHOUT AN EXPLICIT 'bd import' (2026-07-25). bd installs tracked hooks at .beads/hooks/post-checkout and .beads/hooks/post-merge that run 'bd hooks run <hook>', which re-imports .beads/issues.jsonl into the Dolt DB. So the mayor's merge routine 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads && git pull --ff-only' does TWO destructive things: the checkout reverts the export (losing any close since the last commit), and then the post-checkout/post-merge hook writes that STALE file back INTO the database, reopening beads that were legitimately closed. Removing my explicit 'bd import' was only half the fix — the hooks do it automatically. CONFIRMED on rf2-a32r7 (closed three times, zero AUDIT-REOPEN notes, resurrected each time) and rf2-kqxe6.17. CORRECT MERGE/CHECKPOINT SEQUENCE — COMMIT BEFORE PULL, never checkout-before-pull: (1) bd export --all -o .beads/issues.jsonl  (2) guard wc -l >= 2000  (3) git add .beads/issues.jsonl && git commit  (4) git pull --rebase  (5) if issues.jsonl conflicts: git checkout --theirs, bd import it, bd export, commit — the documented resolve-then-regenerate, which is the ONE legitimate use of import  (6) git push. Never 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads' while the DB holds uncommitted closes. If a pull must be unblocked, commit the export first. DIAGNOSTIC: a procedure-revert has ZERO AUDIT-REOPEN / MERGED-PR AUDIT notes and reads pre-close; a genuine reviewer reopen names an unmet defect at a code site. Grep before re-closing.

RUNNING THE LANE AN AUDIT COULD NOT RUN OVERTURNED THE AUDIT ITSELF (2026-07-26, rf2-drpa3.182.4 defect 3).

MERGED-PR AUDIT #7095 found that controls/composing? ORs three independent signals — event.isComposing, keyCode == 229, nativeEvent.isComposing — while press-enter! set BOTH isComposing true AND keyCode 229 on one event, so an implementation reading only isComposing stayed green and the Chromium fallback was never exercised. Its prescribed fix: make each of the three OR branches independently falsifiable. The audit stated plainly that it COULD NOT RERUN THE BROWSER LANE because shadow-cljs was not installed in its environment, so its finding was reasoned from the test event and the shipped OR.

THE WORKER RAN THAT LANE, AND THE THREE-BRANCH PREMISE WAS WRONG. Disabling (.-isComposing e) on the SYNTHETIC event reds NOTHING — React does not forward the flag — while disabling the nativeEvent read withholds nothing. So the OR named TWO COORDINATE SIGNALS, one of them UNREACHABLE under every shipped Freehand host, because the substrate is React-only.

THE HONEST FIX WAS THEREFORE NOT THREE FALSIFIABLE BRANCHES. It is ONE SIGNAL WITH TWO SURFACES — nativeEvent for a React host, the event itself for a raw DOM one — plus the keyCode sentinel. Truth value unchanged for every input; the docstring now describes what the code can actually observe. Each remaining signal IS independently falsifiable, proved one at a time: disabling the standard flag reds only the flag row, disabling the 229 sentinel reds only the fallback row, one failure each.

THE GENERAL RULE, and it is the sharpest form of verify-the-verifier this artefact has produced: AN AUDIT THAT NAMES ITS OWN UNRUN GATE IS TELLING YOU WHICH PART OF ITS FINDING IS INFERENCE. Read that admission as a pointer, not as a caveat. Where an audit says "I could not run X, so this follows from reading the code", the FIRST thing the fixing worker should do is run X — because the reading can be right about the defect and wrong about its shape, which is exactly what happened: the vacuous-test finding was real, the three-branch model was not.

COROLLARY FOR MY BRIEFS: when I dispatch an audit residual whose audit records an unrun gate, say so explicitly and instruct the worker to run it FIRST. I did tell this worker "you should actually run it" and that instruction is what produced the correction. Keep it.

PROCESS NOTE WORTH KEEPING: the same worker also proved defect 1 by reverting a predicate to contains? and observing 6 failures ALL NAMING ITS OWN NEW TEST and NOTHING ELSE IN A 1207-TEST SUITE — which is the direct measurement of the audit claim that prior coverage was blind. A mutation that reds only your new test is how you prove the gap was real rather than asserted.

SENDMESSAGE'S OWN RESPONSE IS A RELIABLE WORKER-LIVENESS SIGNAL (discovered 2026-07-25, after four incidents that a reliable signal would have prevented).

The two response shapes mean different things:
  * 'Message queued for delivery to <id> at its next tool round.' => the agent is ALIVE and mid-task. Do not prune its worktree, do not assume its beads are discharged.
  * 'Agent "<id>" had no active task; resumed from transcript in the background with your message.' => the agent was IDLE/COMPLETE at that moment. Its worktree was prunable, and whatever it had was final.

WHY THIS MATTERS: terminality was the fact I kept lacking. I pruned three worktrees from under live workers by inferring done-ness from 'PR merged' plus a clean tree, and I merged two PRs mid-push for the same reason — the merge sweep has PR state in hand while liveness lives in task notifications that arrive asynchronously and repeat (a background agent notifies every time it stops with no live children, so one job notifies several times and 'completed' does NOT mean finished). Freshness helps but is a stale sample: a worker 45 minutes quiet turned out to be mid-write and committed 3 seconds after I looked.

HOW TO USE IT: when terminality is ambiguous and the decision is destructive or finalising (prune, close a bead, treat a merge as complete), send the worker a short status question and READ THE TOOL'S OWN RESPONSE. That is cheap, non-destructive, and definitive at the moment you ask. It also does something useful either way: an alive worker gets your update, an idle one gets resumed with it.

Note the resume side effect: messaging an idle agent RESTARTS it from its transcript. That is usually desirable (it picks up remaining work with fresh context on what changed), but it means the check is not free — do not poll with it, and do not use it on an agent whose work you want left finished.

SEVENTH FALSE-GREEN VECTOR: STALE SHADOW-CLJS CACHE ON AN .EDN-ONLY EDIT (2026-07-25, found by the EP-0037 routing worker). conformance-fixtures INLINES the EDN at compile time and declares no cache dependency on the .edn file — so editing ONLY a fixture .edn does not invalidate the shadow-cljs cache, and the suite recompiles from cache and reports the OLD fixture's verdict. The worker's failing CLJS conformance fixture was this, not a real failure. CI never sees it because CI compiles fresh from a cold cache; it bites LOCAL runs only, which is the worst shape — a worker debugging a red it cannot explain, or worse, a worker whose fixture fix appears not to work and who then 'fixes' something that was never broken.

WORKAROUND: after an .edn-only fixture edit, clear .shadow-cljs (or touch a .cljs/.cljc file in the same build) before believing a local CLJS result. Related known trap: a stale shadow-cljs SERVER JVM after a source-dir rename produces 'namespace not available' — check .shadow-cljs/server.pid age and kill the java pid.

THE FULL LIST OF WAYS A GREEN LIES IN THIS REPO, now seven: (1) piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's status; (2) a compound or backgrounded command's trailing echo supplies a 0 while the log says FAIL — this worker hit it TWICE in one session and caught both by rc capture; (3) test-fast-pr.sh soft-skips its own mkdocs step when mkdocs is off PATH and still exits 0; (4) a .cljc test namespace missing its lane suffix is silently skipped by one runner; (5) a wrapper-reported 'exit code 0' disagreeing with a captured rc; (6) the BACKGROUNDING HARNESS reporting exit code 0 for a run whose log says rc=1; (7) this one — a stale compile cache serving an old inlined fixture.

Note that (7) is different in kind from (1)-(6): those are about MISREADING a verdict, this is about the verdict being computed from stale INPUT. So 'capture rc and cross-check the log' does not catch it. The brief line that does: 'an .edn/data-only edit may not invalidate the CLJS cache — clear .shadow-cljs before trusting a local CLJS result on a data-only change.'

When a worker edits a test namespace then runs node tests, shadow-cljs incremental compile can show a PHANTOM failure referencing the PRE-EDIT test source (a compile race). Fix: force a clean 'npx shadow-cljs compile node-test' before trusting 'node out/node-test.js'. Seen by rf2-2lb7z worker (PR #1946) — first two runs showed a stale 1-failure, clean recompile gave 0. Tell test-authoring workers to recompile-then-run after editing a test ns.

BOTH /tmp AND THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD ARE SHARED ACROSS CONCURRENT AGENTS ON THIS HOST. Two independent workers hit this on 2026-07-24, in two different directories.

INSTANCE 1 — /tmp: a worker gate log written to /tmp/gate-browser.log was overwritten by ANOTHER worker run. It read EXIT=0 and "0 failures" — plausible numbers, wrong code. The only tell was the shadow-cljs "config:" banner naming a different worktree. This defeats the capture-and-echo-the-exit-code discipline, because the captured EXIT CODE belongs to the other run too.

INSTANCE 2 — THE SCRATCHPAD: the v/->react worker had its pr-body.md OVERWRITTEN by another worker mid-task. Caught before it did damage, but a PR body is exactly the kind of file you write once and read back later without re-checking.

THE RULE, now standard in every brief: write worker-owned files to a WORKTREE-LOCAL path, not /tmp and not a bare name in the shared scratchpad. If the scratchpad must be used, make the filename UNIQUE (include the branch or bead id). And VERIFY OWNERSHIP before believing any captured artefact — for a shadow-cljs run, the "config:" banner names the worktree whose build ran; grep it and confirm it is yours.

GENERAL FORM, which is why this outlives both instances: when an assertion or an artefact rests on something OUTSIDE your process — a shared temp directory, a shared port, a shared cache, a scratchpad — ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read back. A file you wrote is not necessarily the file you read. This is the same family as the console-shim trap (the observer sits below your runtime) and the attribute-order trap (the serialisation carries incidental detail) — in every case the thing being measured is not the thing you think you are measuring.

MAYOR NOTE: my own boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log" for a long stretch of dispatches. Saturating six workers on one machine makes shared-path collision the NORMAL case, not an edge case.

SHARED SCRATCHPAD CAN OVERWRITE A LIVE WORKER'S FILE MID-TASK (2026-07-25, second occurrence, escalating). Concurrent workers share one temp root. First occurrence: a worker reached for scratchpad/pr-body.md and found ANOTHER worker's PR body already in it — caught by a stale-read refusal. Second occurrence: the R6 worker's own scratchpad file was ACTIVELY OVERWRITTEN mid-task by a different PR's body content, and it only noticed because a python string-replace threw on a missing substring. Its own assessment: 'a silent overwrite of a body file could have published the wrong description' — i.e. gh pr edit --body-file could publish another PR's text under your PR.

AGENT-QUALIFIED FILENAMES ARE NOT SUFFICIENT — the second victim was already using them. Brief workers to: (1) write PR bodies inside their OWN WORKTREE (a gitignored path like <worktree>/ai/gate-logs/ or <worktree>/.worker/), never the shared session scratchpad; (2) verify content immediately before publishing — re-read the file and confirm it contains an expected marker unique to THIS PR; (3) treat a string-replace that fails to find its substring as a CORRUPTION SIGNAL, not a bug in the pattern. The R6 worker's recovery is the right pattern: it treated the live PR body on GitHub as the source of truth and rebuilt from that rather than trusting local state.

Related mayor-side trap from the same session: Git Bash /tmp and Windows Python /tmp are DIFFERENT paths. Python raised FileNotFoundError while a following 'gh pr edit --body-file /tmp/...' happily re-uploaded the UNMODIFIED file — a chain that reported success while doing nothing. Gate any publish on the editing step's own return code.

STALE .shadow-cljs CLASSPATH MIMICS THE shadow.resource UNBOUND-VAR RACE — two different causes, one identical error string (2026-07-23).

THE SYMPTOM, identical in both cases: `unbound fn: #(quote shadow.resource/slurp-resource)`, surfacing as a compile failure (seen in scripts/api-manifest/probe/).

CAUSE A — STALE CLASSPATH (benign, one-time): commit 6328dca436 changed the shadow-cljs :source-path classpath root from spec/conformance to spec/. Any worktree with a WARM .shadow-cljs still holds the old classpath.edn and fails this way after pulling that commit. CURE: delete .shadow-cljs in that worktree and recompile (1811 files, 0 warnings observed). Every warm worktree that pulls that commit needs the one-time clear — expect this across a whole wave of workers, not just one.

CAUSE B — THE REAL RACE (rf2-sff2s, recurring as rf2-drpa3.78): requiring-resolve performs its first resolve BEFORE entering the namespace require lock; shadow/resource.clj ships un-AOT-d so it compiles from source on first use, and shadow-cljs macroexpands in parallel — a thread arriving mid-load gets the interned-but-UNBOUND Var. Cured per-consumer by a namespace-local delay, and process-wide by one shared choke point that enters the serialized require path before resolving.

⚠️ WHY THIS PAIRING IS DANGEROUS: a worker fixing the race can read a stale-classpath failure as its bug reproducing, or conclude its fix failed when it actually worked. And a worker hitting the stale classpath can waste a cycle believing it found a concurrency defect.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: a shadow-cljs COMPILE failure is not reliable evidence of the race in either direction. The race must be evidenced by a CONCURRENCY PROBE in a clean Clojure process — one thread cold-loading shadow.resource, an observer resolving the same Var and reporting its state — which observes the Var directly and does not depend on any build. If clearing .shadow-cljs makes the failure vanish, it was Cause A.

MAYOR RULE: when a wave of workers is running warm worktrees and a source-path or classpath-root change lands on main, expect this error across several of them and say so in briefs; do not let it be diagnosed independently five times.

Supersede/amend an existing bead ONLY if it is OPEN and NOT in-progress and NOT closed. A dedupe/supersede match that is IN_PROGRESS (worker is mid-flight and will not see the change) or CLOSED (work is done and will not be re-actioned) must get a NEW bead instead — otherwise the new intent/work is lost. Always verify the candidate status before amending. (Mike, 2026-05-31). Generalises the rule that refinements to an in-progress bead rarely reach the worker.

SUSTAINED API 529 OUTAGE — THE MAYOR PLAYBOOK, learned 2026-07-26 when six workers were killed inside about twenty minutes.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE: task-notifications with status=failed and "API Error: 529 Overloaded", each carrying the worker last sentence — which is usually mid-diagnosis and genuinely valuable. Not stopped for cause, nothing wrong with the work.

THE MISTAKE I MADE FIRST: resuming them. SendMessage-resume during a live outage burns a worker turn and dies on contact — I resumed three and all three died again immediately, one of them twice. Resuming is correct AFTER the window, useless during it. The tell that you are still inside the window is a resumed agent failing within a minute with the same 529.

THE CORRECT POSTURE, in priority order:
1. STOP RESUMING. Each attempt costs a turn and returns nothing. The cron loop will retry; let it.
2. DO NOT DISPATCH NEW WORK. A bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface, and every new worker is another thing to recover.
3. SWITCH TO DURABILITY. Sweep every worktree: for each, compare local HEAD against git ls-remote for its branch, and count uncommitted files excluding .beads. Classify pushed / UNPUSHED / NO-REMOTE. Pushed commits survive anything; uncommitted files survive only as long as nobody reaps the worktree.
4. PROTECT THE AT-RISK ONE ON ITS BEAD. The mayor must NOT commit another worker uncommitted WIP (only that worker knows whether it forms a coherent change). But the mayor DOES control reaping — so the mitigation is to record on the bead that the worktree holds N uncommitted files, name the path and branch, and mark it EXEMPT from the hygiene loop zero-commit/clean/no-PR reap rule. That converts an invisible risk into a written one.
5. Message the still-live workers to commit and push immediately, WITH the reason — a live worker can still act even while resumes of dead ones fail.

FRESHNESS-CHECK TRAP HIT DURING THE SAME PASS, worth its own line: a find over a worktree for recently-touched files reports .beads/* churn, because bd re-exports into EVERY worktree from any worktree. Exclude .beads, .git, node_modules, .shadow-cljs and .cpcache or a cold worktree reads as warm. And even then, a count of ~4500 touched files is an npm ci or an mkdocs build, not liveness — the file COUNT is a proxy for a recent build, not for a running agent. The only reliable liveness signal remains the SendMessage response shape ("queued for delivery" = alive; "had no active task, resumed from transcript" = was idle).

AND THE THING THAT MADE THIS SURVIVABLE: push-as-you-go was already in every brief. Four of seven workers had their commits on origin and lost nothing. The one that was genuinely at risk was the one that had not committed yet. That single instruction is worth more than the entire recovery procedure.

TENTH FALSE-GREEN VARIANT: report-changed-surfaces.sh TAKES PATHS, NOT REFS, AND SILENTLY REPORTS NOTHING CHANGED (2026-07-26, hit by the scaffold-floor worker on itself).

Invoking scripts/.../report-changed-surfaces.sh origin/main treats "origin/main" as a literal FILE PATH. No such path changed, so it prints every surface false and exits successfully — i.e. "your diff touches nothing, no gate needs to run." Re-run on the real changed paths, it correctly armed examples_compile=true. There is no error, no usage message, and no hint that the argument was misread.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE INVOCATION: this is the classifier that decides which CI jobs arm. A caller who passes a ref gets a confident all-false answer, which is exactly the answer that means "skip everything". It is the same failure direction as check-beads-pr-boundary.sh exiting 0 with no base ref — a gate-adjacent script that cannot understand its input and reports the benign case rather than refusing.

DIRECTLY RELEVANT RIGHT NOW: the ci-arming worker is editing this very script to add JVM arms for tools/machines-viz and tools/testbed-support. It must pass real paths when testing its own arms, or it will see all-false and conclude its arm does not work — or worse, conclude the arm works when it has not exercised it.

GENERAL RULE, now with two instances: a script in the gate path that accepts an argument should refuse an argument it cannot interpret, not fall through to the empty result. When touching either of these, prefer making the misuse loud over documenting the correct usage.

TENTH INSTRUMENT FAULT CLASS: A LARGE-OBJECT ARM INFLATES ITS SUCCESSOR BY 2x, REPRODUCIBLY. Measuring narrow-write allocation (rf2-jr76s), an SMI control read 16.1052 B/slot in FORWARD order and 8.0027 B/slot (+0.03% against prediction) in REVERSED order — the only difference being whether an 87 KB arm ran immediately before it. No V8-level diagnosis; filed as rf2-88pie. IT WAS CAUGHT ONLY BY RUNNING BOTH ARM ORDERS, which is now standard practice on this surface and has paid for itself twice. Related large-object effect from the same run: a .slice() control calibrated to +0.56% on a small pair (100->200 doubles) but read +9.11% on a large pair (1000->10000) — V8 page-tail filler. RULE: run every measurement in both arm orders and reconcile; if one order disagrees with the other, the ARM ORDER is a variable and neither number is safe until you know why.

When testing dispatch captures via with-redefs: rf/dispatch is a MACRO that expands to rf/dispatch* (adds :rf.trace/call-site). Redef rf/dispatch* not rf/dispatch — first attempt to redef the macro lets handlers slip through. Captured opts should strip :rf.trace/call-site before assertions. Discovered in rf2-ykjl5 PR #1470 section-header affordance tests.

TEST-RUNNER FALSE GREEN: from implementation/, 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' WITHOUT '-d <dir>' makes the Cognitect runner default to a non-existent ./test and silently report 'Ran 0 tests, 0 assertions' — which READS AS GREEN. Correct form is 'clojure -M:test -d core/test -n <ns>' (adjust the -d dir per artefact). Found by the rf2-8sc64 worker on #6308, 2026-07-18. THIS AFFECTS MAYOR BRIEFS: I have repeatedly written focused-ns gate commands as 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' — any worker that ran exactly that and reported a small/zero test count may have proven nothing. When a worker reports a focused-ns run, CHECK THE TEST COUNT IS NON-ZERO and plausible for the ns; 'Ran 0 tests' or an implausibly small count is a red flag, not a pass. Prefer instructing the FULL artefact suite (clojure -M:test from the artefact dir) over a focused -n, or require the -d flag explicitly.

The 'already landed' grep has a BLIND SPOT: work fixed under a SIBLING bead's id. `git log --grep=<bead-id> origin/main` catches 'this bead was fixed and left open', but NOT 'another bead's PR captured this bead's substance'. rf2-xu6rx (interpreter memo caches -> js/Map) returned nothing for its own id, yet the swap had already merged ~12h earlier in PR #7077 under rf2-lnecd. SECOND CHECK for any bead whose body cites a finding from ANOTHER bead's report: grep the SOURCE for the change itself, not the bead id — here `grep 'js/Map' conversion.cljc` on main would have shown `#?(:cljs (js/Map.) :clj (atom {}))` already present. Rule: when a bead's provenance is 'split out of X' or 'headroom X did not capture', check whether X's own PR later captured it.

THE BASH TOOL SILENTLY STRIPS BACKSLASHES FROM HEREDOC STRINGS ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP (2026-07-26).

Found by the checker-residuals worker while probing a char-literal guard: a heredoc probe string lost its backslashes, so the probe read as a FALSE NEGATIVE — the guard looked broken when the input had been mangled before it arrived. It rewrote every probe as a FILE under its own worktree and the results reversed.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE KNOWN git worktree add BACKSLASH STRIPPING, which is already recorded, but the surface is different and more insidious: a worktree path failing is loud, whereas a mangled PROBE STRING silently changes what you are testing. Any probe involving backslashes, char literals, regex escapes or line continuations must be written to a FILE, not passed through a heredoc.

AND IT COST A REAL VERDICT IN THE SAME SESSION, in a second form: that worker plant C did not apply because of a LINE-CONTINUATION BACKSLASH in the anchor, and the self-test returned rc=0 — INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GATE THAT MISSED THE DEFECT. Only the mandated "confirm the diff applied before reading the verdict" protocol caught it. That is the twelfth false-signal class firing in the wild and being caught by the exact rule written for it.

SO THE RULE COMPOUNDS: for any mutation or probe whose payload contains a backslash, (1) write it to a file rather than a heredoc, and (2) confirm it applied by git diff --stat AND by grepping the token back out. Either check alone would have missed one of the two failures above.

A THIRD FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, unrelated but worth the same memory: a PRIME-SUFFIXED SYMBOL (db-prime, tags-prime) reads as a QUOTE to the bijection walker regex — 352 occurrences in the tree, the same class the existing backslash-quote lookbehind was written for, and a FALSE-GREEN direction. Latent rather than live because all 352 sit inside binding vectors the walk cannot reach. Closed with one lookbehind. The lesson: when a regex already has a lookbehind for one lookalike, ASK WHAT ELSE LOOKS LIKE THAT — the second instance is usually already in the tree.

The core JVM suite (implementation/core clojure -M:test) runs ~10min under concurrent worker/mayor JVM load — right at the 600s foreground tool limit. This is the ROOT of the 'workers strand on backgrounded gates' pattern: a worker can't reliably foreground it when the machine is contended, so it backgrounds the gate + ends its turn with work uncommitted + no PR. Mitigation: briefs must say 'run gates FOREGROUND, do not background; if the core JVM suite risks the 600s limit run a FOCUSED namespace subset (clojure -M:test :only <ns>) not the whole suite'; recover a stranded worker by SendMessage-resume telling it to finish foreground in one turn.

THE CROSS-BASE CHECK: TWO PRs EACH GREEN AGAINST A BASE LACKING THE OTHER CAN STILL BREAK IN COMBINATION (2026-07-26).

A worker did this unprompted and it is the practice I most want to adopt. Its work and PR #7081 were EACH GREEN against a base that did not contain the other. Rather than assume the combination was fine, it built a THROWAWAY WORKTREE AT origin/main WITH BOTH MERGED and ran the suite: freehand JVM 1156/7707, 0F 0E. Then removed the worktree.

WHY THIS MATTERS AT SATURATION: I run up to six workers, each rebasing onto a moving main, and I merge on green. Every green I act on was measured against a base THAT NO LONGER EXISTS by the time I merge. Nineteen PRs today merged a state older than the worker tip; several pairs touched adjacent surfaces. THE MERGE LOOP HAS NO CROSS-BASE SIGNAL AT ALL — CI re-runs on the merge commit, but I do not wait for it.

WHEN TO REQUIRE IT: when two live PRs touch the SAME artefact or adjacent seams — for example one editing implementation/freehand/src and another editing implementation/freehand/test, or two both moving spec/009 rows. It is cheap: one throwaway worktree at origin/main, both branches merged, the ONE suite that spans both surfaces. Not the whole spine.

WHEN NOT TO: disjoint surfaces. Most of the time the fence system already guarantees it, and this would be ceremony.

THE MERGED-PR AUDIT CAN DESTRUCTIVELY OVERWRITE A BEAD'S ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (2026-07-25, found by EP-0037 review gate 2). This is a process defect in a process I do not control, and it silently destroys the only record of what a slice promised.

WHAT HAPPENED: R1's and R2's slice acceptance criteria were REWRITTEN — both the title AND the description — into the audit's follow-through text. PRs #6875/#6877 name rf2-kqxe6.5/.6 as the slice owners; their original criteria no longer exist anywhere. By contrast the audits of .3 and .7 APPENDED their findings, leaving the criteria intact. That difference is exactly why an independent completeness review could verify .3 and .7 and could NOT verify .5 and .6. Named casualty: the R2 tooling clause ended up with no bead at all.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE EPIC: acceptance criteria are the only durable record of what was promised. A merged-PR audit's job is to record what it found, and it is very good at that — it caught a keyword-as-Var false green, a load-order privacy defect, a declared-:on-* classification defect and a census extent bug. But an audit that overwrites the promise it is auditing removes the ability to check completeness later, and the loss is invisible: the bead still reads coherently, just as the audit's narrative rather than as the slice's contract.

MAYOR ACTIONS: (1) treat audit notes as APPEND-ONLY when I write them myself, and say so in briefs — findings go in notes, never over a description; (2) when a bead's description reads as audit narrative rather than as acceptance criteria, suspect this and check git history of .beads for the original; (3) rf2-twpp6 tracks the append-only repair for the two affected beads; (4) when commissioning a completeness review, tell it that a bead whose criteria were overwritten is UNVERIFIABLE and should be reported as such rather than passed — gate 2 worked this out unprompted and it is the reason its verdict is trustworthy.

GENERALISABLE FORM: any automated process that writes into the tracker can destroy the state a later reviewer needs. Prefer append. If a tool overwrites, the tracker's git history is the only recovery path — which is another reason the .beads export must keep being committed on the heartbeat.

THE MID-WRITE RACE ACTUALLY FIRED TODAY AND AN EMPTY EXPORT REACHED main (2026-07-26).

WHAT HAPPENED: commit 4d8042d80d ("chore(beads): audit merged PR #7063") committed .beads/issues.jsonl AT ZERO ROWS. The previous commit d1c49b1164 had 2573. The working tree, the index and HEAD were all empty and git status was CLEAN, so nothing looked wrong — the file simply was not there any more.

THE DATABASE WAS NEVER AT RISK. Dolt is the source of truth; bd list returned every bead normally throughout. Recovery was one command: scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, which runs bd export and REGENERATES from Dolt rather than trusting the working file, then refuses an empty or badly shrunken result. It committed 2576 rows over a HEAD of 0. That refusal-plus-regenerate design is exactly why the script exists instead of a hand-rolled git add.

THE MECHANISM, now observed rather than theorised: a process ran git add on the export WHILE a bd operation was rewriting it, and snapshotted the zero-length intermediate. I hit the same window myself twenty minutes earlier — read the export as 0 rows with bd.exe alive — and did NOT commit, which is the only reason my own pass was clean. The audit process hit it and did commit.

TWO RULES THAT FOLLOW, and the first is cheap enough to be unconditional:
  1. GUARD EVERY CHECKPOINT ON A ROW COUNT. Never commit the export without asserting it is above a floor (2000+ here). The checkpoint script already does this; anything else that touches the file must too.
  2. AN EMPTY EXPORT IS NOT A DATA LOSS EVENT — IT IS A REGENERATION EVENT. Do not panic-restore from git history: git checkout of an older export would TIME-TRAVEL THE TRACKER, reopening closed beads and vanishing new ones. Always regenerate from Dolt.

AND A DETECTION NOTE: I nearly reported "0 open beads" as a real number. The tell was that it disagreed with the previous pass by 49. WHEN A COUNT MOVES TO ZERO, SUSPECT THE INSTRUMENT BEFORE THE WORLD — that is the tenth measurement error of this class I have caught today, and the only one that would have been consequential.

THE REOPEN TAXONOMY HAS A THIRD CLASS, AND I MISSED IT TWICE (2026-07-26).

I recorded two classes: (A) WEAK-CLOSE reopens, where the close said the job was ARMED rather than CATCHING and the audit had nothing to verify against — mine to prevent; and (B) NEW-RESIDUAL reopens, where a fully-evidenced close was accepted and the audit found something ELSE in the merged code — the audit working as designed.

THE REOPENS WORKER FOUND A THIRD, and it is distinct from both: (C) THE CLOSE ITSELF INTRODUCED THE DEFECT. rf2-12g5z was reopened against PR #7028 OWN NEW TEXT — spec/Privacy.md claimed "every production error record shipped off-box carries one too", which is false because error_emit.cljc:216 returns nil for three shapes and the emitter conditionally assocs the slot. The audit ACCEPTED the original finding and objected to the prose the fix added. In the worker words: "neither residual missed nor original re-asserted".

WHY C MATTERS SEPARATELY: A is a discipline failure I can fix by writing better close reasons. B is discovery I cannot reduce. C IS A REVIEW GAP — the fix was right and its accompanying claim was wrong, which no amount of close-reason rigour catches, because the close reason is describing a fix that IS correct. The remedy is different again: when a fix adds NEW PROSE asserting a general property, that prose needs the same evidence standard as the code. A sentence like "every production record carries X" is a UNIVERSAL CLAIM and should be checked against the conditional that emits X.

AND A FOURTH BUCKET THAT IS NOT A REOPEN AT ALL: rf2-ia904 reads like a reopen of rf2-2z9u3 but was FILED NEW by the #7042 audit. rf2-2z9u3 stays correctly closed. So "the bead is open again" has at least four causes and only one of them is my fault. Before treating an open-looking bead as a reopen, ASK WHICH OF THE FOUR IT IS — the worker did this per bead and it changed what each one owed.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THE BACKLOG NUMBER: I have been reporting roughly one reopen per merged PR as partly my defect. The honest split is now: A is mine, B and D are the system working, and C is a review gap that belongs to whoever wrote the accompanying prose. Only A responds to better closing.

The skill↔MCP drift gate has TWO distinct failure modes — do NOT assume flake (learned 2026-07-18, rf2-92dlh). (1) The TRANSIENT flake: 'Verify skill ↔ MCP allowed-tools drift' fails under concurrent-PR load; structurally impossible when the diff has 0 skills/MCP files → --admin-justifiable. (2) A REAL main-red drift: when a PR adds/changes MCP server tools WITHOUT reconciling the consumer skills' allowed-tools + the retro drift-set, check_skill_mcp_drift.py --ci reports real findings and the gate is RED ON MAIN — every subsequent PR inherits that red. I conflated the two: rf2-vxgfnd.95.8 added 5 re-frame2-pair MCP tools (explain-render/read-view-*) without updating skills/re-frame2-pair/SKILL.md allowed-tools + scripts/check_skill_mcp_drift.py's re-frame2-pair-retro intentional_server_only set, so main's drift gate went REAL-red — and I kept --admin-ing PRs past it as 'the flake' for many merges until .95.10's spine run surfaced it (rf2-92dlh). FIX GOING FORWARD: when the drift gate is red, VERIFY main's own drift state — run/check  (or check main's gate run). If it exits non-zero (real findings), it is NOT a flake — file/dispatch a fix (allow-list the new tools in SKILL.md + the retro drift-set) instead of --admin-ing PRs past it. Only --admin when main's drift gate is GREEN and the PR's red is the load flake (0 skills/MCP diff).

The test asserts parsed-always-on-set-equals-the-exercise-literal — a catalogue always-on row with no matching literal entry fails with only-in-catalogue: (:the-new-id).

⚠️ AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FLAKE HEURISTIC: I diagnosed this as a CI flake because "the diff touches 0 files under implementation/core/ and JVM core is green on main." THAT REASONING IS WRONG for cross-artefact conformance tests. The real touched surface was spec/009-Instrumentation.md (the catalogue), which the PR DID touch; a CORE test parses that shared spec file and compares it to a literal. So "diff has no core SOURCE files" does NOT imply "core gate cannot be affected" — a gate in artefact A can read a shared artefact-agnostic file (spec/009, Spec-Schemas, Conventions) that the diff edited. The flake signature must be: diff cannot affect the failing gate THROUGH ANY PATH INCLUDING SHARED SPEC FILES A GATE PARSES — not merely "no source files of that artefact in the diff." I nearly --admin-merged past a genuine touched-surface gate. The rule holds: a failing touched-surface gate is NEVER an --admin candidate; when unsure whether it is touched, READ THE FAILURE (it named the test, the file, the exact only-in-catalogue id) before concluding flake.

THE ui JVM ASSERTION COUNT IS NONDETERMINISTIC; THE TEST COUNT IS NOT. ⚠️ CONSEQUENCE FOR EVERY BRIEF I WRITE: I have been telling workers "counts must be non-zero AND PLAUSIBLE" and quoting expected assertion totals (~18660, ~18744, etc). For implementation/ui those assertion numbers CANNOT be used as a precise expectation — only as an order-of-magnitude sanity check. Pin expectations to TEST counts, not assertion counts, for any suite containing concurrency tests. A worker who sees an assertion count differ by a handful from my quoted figure should NOT treat that as a finding; a worker who sees the TEST count differ should.
This also retro-explains earlier session confusion where assertion totals drifted run-to-run (16136/16141/16143 on an identical tree) — same cause, and the right response then and now is: use test counts as the stable signal.

GATE LOGS MUST NOT GO TO /tmp UNDER MULTI-AGENT LOAD — /tmp is SHARED across concurrently running worker agents on this box, so one worker gate log silently OVERWRITES another. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.112 SSR worker, which nearly shipped a false green.

THE MECHANISM: worker A runs "npm run test:browser > /tmp/gate-browser.log 2>&1". Worker B, running concurrently in a DIFFERENT worktree, writes the same path. A then reads a log that is really B run. In the observed case the log EXIT=0 and reported "0 failures" — every number looked right. The ONLY tell was the shadow-cljs banner naming the WRONG worktree (pilot-react-interop-46 instead of the reader own).

WHY THIS IS NASTY: it defeats the standard exit-code discipline. The capture-to-a-file-and-echo-the-exit-code rule was adopted precisely because piping into tail/grep discards the runner exit status. But if the FILE ITSELF belongs to another agent, the captured exit code is ALSO another agent — a correct technique reading the wrong evidence. Both the summary AND the exit code agree, and both are about someone else run.

THE FIX, now standard in every dispatch brief: write gate logs to the SESSION SCRATCHPAD or a worktree-local path, never a bare /tmp name. e.g.
  <gate> > "$WT/gate-<name>.log" 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -30 "$WT/gate-<name>.log"
And VERIFY OWNERSHIP: the shadow-cljs "config:" banner line names the worktree whose build ran. Grep it and confirm it is YOURS before believing any number in that file. That is the cheap proof.

MAYOR NOTE: my own standing gate-discipline boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log". That instruction is now known-unsafe whenever more than one worker runs at a time, which is the normal case at saturation. Update the boilerplate; do not keep handing workers a colliding path.

GENERAL FORM: this joins the roster of ways green has meant nothing-was-measured here. The others are about a check that could not fail; this one is about a check that MEASURED SOMEBODY ELSE. When an assertion rests on an artefact OUTSIDE your process (a shared temp file, a shared port, a shared cache), ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read.

TRUE-CONCLUSION-DEAD-REASONING — a documented defect class, seen twice on 2026-07-19 and subtler than plain drift.

DEFINITION: a document states a correct conclusion resting on an inference that has since been invalidated. Nothing looks wrong — the conclusion checks out — so a reviewer confirms the conclusion and moves on. But the NEXT reader follows the stated reason, finds it false, and "corrects" the conclusion in the wrong direction. The rot is in the justification, not the claim.

INSTANCE 1 (rf2-0qsp5, #6386): spec/005-StateMachines.md derived :rf.machine/join-dispatch target protection FROM its REJECT-tier membership. Worker verdict: "The conclusion is true; the inference is precisely what the split invalidated." Preserving the reasoning would have re-merged the two fx policies the next time anyone extended it.

INSTANCE 2 (rf2-vxgfnd.188, #6391, worse): the canonical W1 rule table declared SEVEN verbs unavailable — ui/adapter, local, effect, ui/event, ui/handler, ui/render-fn, ui/dispatch-fn. ALL SEVEN SHIP, exported from ui.cljc. MIG-16/17/18 "this gates" conclusions stayed TRUE, but the reason inverted: from "the verb has not shipped yet" to "the decision belongs to the human". Retiering alone would have let the next reader check whether S3 shipped, find it had, and UNGATE RULES THAT MUST STAY GATED. The worker rewrote the reasons and left the tiers.

HOW TO CATCH IT: when reconciling a document against code, verify the DERIVATION, not just the conclusion. Ask "if the stated reason were false, would the conclusion change?" If yes and the reason IS false, the conclusion is correct by luck and the next edit will break it.
HOW TO FIX IT: rewrite the reason, keep the conclusion. Do NOT retier/restate/delete the conclusion just because its stated basis collapsed.

RELATED, SAME FAMILY: a bead PREDICTION can be wrong too. rf2-vxgfnd.188 own preliminary map predicted six rule retirements; ALL SIX were refuted against shipped code (one, R-X7, had NO DETECTOR AT ALL and became a new rule; R-S3 was missing the cursor WRITE side). A worker trusting the bead analysis would have deleted six live rules. The bead is authoritative about WHAT TO DO, never about WHAT IS TRUE — always re-verify its factual claims against the code.

ALSO: my brief framed 36-vs-34 rules as "one book has two rules the other lacks". Wrong — the books cut the same work at different GRANULARITIES (one by construct area, one by detector), many-to-many both ways, so the deliverable was a crosswalk not a diff. When two artefacts disagree on a COUNT, check whether they share a unit before assuming they disagree on content.

TRUTHFUL-BUT-LATE vs FABRICATED — the discriminator for unfenced async writes. Established by the rf2-2amkm worker (#6410) when it RE-VERIFIED rather than inherited a judgement rf2-6pfpt (#6405) had left.

THE TEST: when a callback settles after its subject is gone, ask whether the value it writes is TRUE-BUT-STALE or FABRICATED-ABOUT-NOTHING.
  - TRUTHFUL-BUT-LATE: runner-events/run-step! emits an unfenced emit-trace! for an abandoned stepper session. The step REALLY RAN and REALLY produced that result; only the timing is wrong. #6410 checked every trace listener under tools/story/src and none consumes :rf.story.play/step. Verdict: LEAVE UNFENCED. Fencing it would mean inventing session identity for a public one-shot executor whose recorded verdict is already fenced caller-side.
  - FABRICATED: the a11y sites. (swap! run-state assoc frame-id :done) over a map the frame was dissoc-d from RESURRECTS the entry — measured 10/10 RED with 19 failures and ZERO ERRORS, so nothing throws. The phantom slot reads :done and the resurrected violations-by-frame entry beside it is exactly what browser/register-a11y-reader! serves to :rf.assert/a11y — A TORN-DOWN FRAME REPORTING A CLEAN VERDICT. Same defect shape, opposite correct action. Do not blanket-fence every unfenced .then; ask what the write ASSERTS.

MECHANISM REFINEMENT worth copying: #6410 stamped the run token INTO the slot rather than beside it, so "existence and identity are one question with one answer, and every present and future clearing path revokes the claim with no side atom to keep in step". Strictly better than a parallel token map, which a new clearing path can silently fail to update.

⚠️ (inc nil) IS 1 ON CLJS. That is why this class never throws — it silently rebuilds state instead. Never test for it by expecting an exception; assert the slot is ABSENT and the status is the terminal value.

DC-09 TWO-CLOCK ENVELOPE, MEASURED (rf2-drpa3.182.12, PR #7179, HeadlessChrome 147, dev build :optimizations :none goog.DEBUG true). Sustained semantic rate ~190/s at 0 dirty siblings, ~49/s at 200. 60 Hz crossing is comfortable to 50 siblings and breaks between 50 and 200; 120 Hz never clears p95 in a dev build; 240 Hz is unreachable because the BROWSER stops offering first, not because the framework refuses.

THREE STRUCTURAL FACTS worth reusing before re-measuring anything on this surface:
1. PEAK BACKLOG IS 1, at every offered rate and both sibling loads, with rf/dispatch (async). The setInterval callback IS the main thread, so overload manifests as OFFER LOSS at the host, never as a growing queue; latency stays bounded at one crossing and the settlement tail stayed <=5.4 ms even at 240 Hz requested against a 20 ms crossing. This is why no throttle/debounce/coalesce verb is warranted — the browser already back-pressures. CAVEAT: measured with a TIMER. Coalesced pointermove / pointerrawupdate bursts can deliver several events to one task and are the only shape that could exceed backlog 1; do not quote this for raw-pointer bursts without re-measuring.
2. THE EVENT HALF IS FLAT, THE COMMIT HALF SCALES. Splitting the window at the instant dispatch-sync returns: :event-ms (router, interceptors, reducer, app-db install, 300 subscription notifications) is 3-4 ms whether 1 or 201 cells moved; :commit-ms goes 0.4 -> 17.5 ms at ~0.085 ms per dirtied cell. An expensive crossing is expensive in React, not in re-frame — attribute before optimising.
3. WHERE YOU READ THE SUB COSTS MORE THAN HOW MUCH CHANGED. Reading a high-rate value in a view that ALSO builds a collection costs a CONSTANT 40-44 ms more than reading it one boundary down — independent of payload size (Vega 96 leaves 45.6->5.0 ms, Spread 900 leaves 63->18.8 ms) — while moving THREE FEWER DOM nodes. Same 'one leaf of app-db changed', 8-19x apart. Guidance: if a high-rate value must cross into app-db, read its subscription at the boundary that USES it.

EQUALITY IS FREE AND FREEHAND ALREADY ELIDES. Fresh-but-rf=-equal is indistinguishable from stable-reference (0.2-0.3 ms at 96 leaves, 0.4-0.6 at 900) and repaints nothing; a full structural walk of a 900-leaf map is under a millisecond. Behavior :update ran exactly 52 times for 52 changed crossings and ZERO times for stable or fresh-equal ones — elision is VALUE-based (rf=), not identity-based. Proved by counting, not by reading the runtime. No equality hook is warranted.

INSTRUMENT NOTES for the next perf bead in a browser:
* A COMPUTED-DURATION POSITIVE CONTROL DOUBLES AS A CONTENTION METER. A busy-wait of exactly 4.00 ms riding in every cell read p50 4.0 with overshoot never above 0.3 ms — which is what let the numbers be published without the usual 'other agents were running' caveat. On a loaded box it would have said so in every table simultaneously. Cheap, and it retires the standing wall-clock-is-unreliable worry per-run instead of per-repo.
* A COMPUTED-SIZE CONTROL CATCHES A KNOB THAT DOES NOT TURN. Predicted DOM mutation counts (host-only 1, fresh-equal 0, one-leaf k+1) matched measured at all 15 mode x rung combinations, and the driven arm independently reproduced exactly 201.0 per crossing. MutationObserver.takeRecords() answers SYNCHRONOUSLY, which is the only reason it can be read inside a flushSync-bracketed window.
* AN ARM WHOSE POINT IS THAT NOTHING CHANGES CANNOT BE VERIFIED BY NOTHING CHANGING. The fresh-equal arm is verified at the STORE (reference moved AND value equal), because an arm that silently did nothing would otherwise be the fastest arm in the table.
* ROTATING ARM ORDER FOUND A REAL FAULT: the first equality arm built its config from a FIXED generation, so a fresh-equal crossing following a one-leaf one was equal to nothing and failed its own read-back in 7 of every 10 samples. Build the comparison value from WHATEVER IS CURRENTLY IN THE STORE, and build it OUTSIDE the timed window.
* BOTH LADDER ORDERS: the only non-overlapping range tracked a monotonic round-1-to-4 warm-up present at EVERY rung in BOTH orders — drift, not order. Three warm-up samples per cell did not fully absorb first-round JIT.
* prov/result REFUSES a record with no revision, and the :browser-test lane has none. Do not route around it: catch the refusal and publish :d021 :not-release-evidence with the reason, so the same rows can run in the ordinary gate AND in the focused bench build with RF2_REVISION set.
* Chrome clamps performance.now() to 100 us. A sub-0.1 ms arm reads 0.0 and its honest report is 'under 0.1 ms', never 'free'.

TWO FREEHAND ADAPTER FACTS the rf2-vo8fb conformance found that reading could not (PR #6948, 2026-07-25):

1. A CLJS NAMESPACE AND A VAR CANNOT SHARE A JS PATH. The bead specified an internal ns 're-frame.freehand.adapter' alongside the published var 'v/adapter'. The compiler emits :ns-var-clash and ONE OF THE TWO SILENTLY READS nil — observed live: v/adapter installed fine while the test namespace's own reference read nil, so the fixture installed nothing and every assertion failed for the wrong reason. Homed at re-frame.freehand.substrate instead (the same split the donor arrived at). The ruled AUTHORING name is unaffected. Generalise: never name an internal namespace the same as a published var in its parent ns.

2. ADAPTER DISPOSAL MUST BE REFERENCE-RELEASE, NOT FRAME DESTROY, and the bug was CLASSPATH-DEPENDENT. Core's claim-installed-for-dispose! sets :disposing? and closes public delegation BEFORE calling the adapter's :dispose-adapter!, so every read-container inside that window raises :rf.error/adapter-disposed — and a frame's destroy recipe reads the runtime-db container. On a classpath WITHOUT the machines artefact that read IS the fallback path, so the defect was latent for some apps and fatal for others. Correct shape: drain-live-roots! releases claims + the frame REFERENCE + the ViewCells, while v/unmount! on a live adapter still destroys a root-owned frame; both share one tear-down-root! differing only in that function. The drain is the safety net for a FORGOTTEN root outliving the adapter, not a substitute for orderly teardown. Conformance carries two rows of different strength rather than one overclaiming row.

TWO GENERALISABLE FINDINGS FROM THE CI-COVERAGE WORK (2026-07-26, PR #7068).

1. WHEN AN INCLUSIVE PATH FILTER WOULD BE THE WHOLE REPOSITORY, DELETE THE FILTER — DO NOT EXTEND IT. rf2-kx06s asked to add two omitted files to a workflow push-path filter. The worker found the two-line fix "correct and incomplete": NEITHER checker in that job has a filterable read universe — one scans every spec/**/*.md, the other runs git ls-files over the WHOLE TREE. So any honest filter is the repository, and a filter that lists paths is a promise the job cannot keep. It deleted the push filter. The workflow OWN paragraph already said the job "belongs on an unfiltered job" while the trigger still carried one.

THE GENERAL RULE: before adding a path to a filter, ask WHAT THE JOB ACTUALLY READS. If the read universe is unbounded, the filter is not incomplete — it is WRONG IN KIND, and every future addition to it is a false sense of coverage. This is the same family as the roster-that-rots, one level up: a maintained LIST OF TRIGGERS rather than a maintained list of members.

2. A CROSS-TREE TEST-HELPER ALIAS MEANS AN EDGE THE BEAD WILL NOT NAME. TWO HEAP-INSTRUMENT TRAPS, both caught by a positive control (rf2-9oj7v, PR #7146). (1) CDP `getHeapUsage` and `performance.memory` are TWO DOORS ONTO ONE V8 COUNTER — they agreed to the byte (3,868,954 both), which LOOKS like independent corroboration and is not. A heap SNAPSHOT is the genuinely independent third reading. (2) A 4.7 MB positive control built as `'x'.repeat(n)` read as SIX KILOBYTES on all three readers — V8 does not materialise it the way you expect, and it would have looked exactly like a broken instrument rather than a broken control. TWO MAYOR ERRORS THE rf2-n4by4 WORKER CAUGHT, BOTH ABOUT MY BRIEFS (2026-07-26).

ERROR 1 — I SILENTLY RESOLVED A RULING THE BEAD HAD EXPLICITLY RESERVED. rf2-n4by4 said in as many words: "ENFORCEMENT NEEDS A RULING — do not pick one silently", and listed (a) mark-and-refuse versus (b) leave it to the spec. My brief supplied (a) as though it were settled. The worker followed the brief and FLAGGED THE DIVERGENCE, noting that per my own standing instruction the bead is authoritative over the brief.

That is the sharpest form of a mistake I make often: I put "the bead is authoritative over this brief, and tell me if they disagree" into every dispatch, which is right — and then write briefs that quietly overwrite the bead. The instruction only works if I read the bead for RESERVED QUESTIONS before writing the brief, not just for facts. A bead that says "needs a ruling" is addressed TO ME, and the honest brief either states the ruling AS a ruling ("I am ruling (a), here is why") or asks the worker to return the options. Silently picking one means the tracker never records that a decision was made, and the next reader cannot tell a considered choice from an oversight.

THE RULING ITSELF STANDS, and the reason is worth keeping: the failure is SILENT — :className arriving as :class is a DIFFERENT React prop, so the component gets no class and nothing reports it. Guard warranted. And the cost turned out near zero: the author spelling rides in METADATA, refused at one seam, with =, hash and pr-str all ignoring it, so the legal element use pays nothing. But I could not have known the cost when I ruled, which is exactly why the ruling should have been visible.

ERROR 2 — MY COLLISION WARNING WAS A GREP, AND TWO OF FOUR HITS WERE FALSE POSITIVES. I warned that four test files contained both "spread" and "defhost" and might pin the accepting behaviour, so the flips had to ride in the same PR. NONE of the four pinned it. Two matched on "SPREADSHEET" and "SPREADJS". One already asserted the CORRECT behaviour (an earlier PR had landed that flip). The fourth was the digest gate, whose spread-forms row points at an element-level fixture.

So a plausible-sounding hazard cost the worker a verification pass it did not need. The mutually-invalidating-test rule is real and has reddened the trunk before — but a bare token grep is not evidence FOR it. Before warning about a witness collision, check whether the match is the CONSTRUCT or merely the SUBSTRING, and whether the assertion pins the old behaviour or the new. Sixteenth instance this session of the same underlying error: a cheap proxy standing in for the real question.

AND THE FINDING MY BRIEF SHOULD HAVE CARRIED, which the worker found instead: THE REFUSAL MUST RUN BEFORE THE EXACTNESS LAW. A spread canonicalises "class" into the keyword :class, so inexact-host-prop-names sees a CLEAN call — exactness would PASS and the corruption would be the answer. Ordering, not presence, is what makes that guard work. Generalise: when adding a check to a pipeline of checks, ask what the earlier checks NORMALISE, because a normaliser upstream can launder exactly the defect you are trying to catch.

TWO VACUOUS-PASS TRAPS WHEN MOVING TESTS UNDER A PRODUCTION GATE (rf2-d2841, PR #7142). Both make a suite report GREEN while proving nothing, and neither is visible in a passing run. (1) A NEGATIVE trace assertion — `empty?` / `not-any?` over a trace ring — passes automatically under `-Dre-frame.debug=false` because the ring is empty BY DESIGN. It must move INSIDE the dev-only guard with the positive assertions, not be left outside as 'posture-independent'. Same for any 'no :rf.error/... was emitted' read. (2) A namespace that is 100% dev instrumentation (trace-listener-*, trace-test, db-pending-trace-test, sub-dispose-trace-test) has NO semantic residue: guarding it wholesale and removing its exclusion-roster line makes the lane report green for a namespace that EXECUTED NOTHING. Those need a var-level tag (`-e :requires-debug`) so the runner skips them explicitly rather than running an empty shell. GENERAL RULE: when a gate's whole point is that instrumentation is absent, any assertion whose subject is that same absence is worthless in that posture — check what each assertion would do if its subject simply never existed.

Untracking a gitignored-but-force-added path via 'git rm --cached' in a SEPARATE worker worktree then merging to main DELETES the files from the mayor checkout's disk on pull — because the resulting commit is a plain file-deletion, and 'git pull' removes working-tree copies of files a commit deletes (the --cached keep-on-disk only protected the worker's tree, which didn't have the files). Recovery: 'git show <pre-untrack-sha>:<path> > <path>' to restore each file as untracked local content (they're gitignored so git ignores them). Better approach next time: do the 'git rm --cached' + commit in the SAME checkout that holds the files (but the mayor hook forbids that), OR restore the files immediately after the untrack merge.

Before dispatching any bead >24h old, run: gh pr list --search '<bead-id>' AND/OR gh issue view <linked-gh-N>. Two dispatches in last hour (migration cluster + rf2-ihzz9) hit already-shipped work. The bootstrap.md 'Before dispatching' grep rule should explicitly include gh search not just codebase grep.

WHAT THE MERGED-PR AUDIT REOPENS, MEASURED — AND IT IS A DEFECT IN MY CLOSE REASONS, NOT IN THE AUDIT (2026-07-26).

THE MEASUREMENT. Of the open beads carrying audit-reopen language, the largest cluster by type is TEST / FIXTURE / GATE beads — 7 of 16, ahead of donor (4), spec-prose (3) and privacy (3). All 16 name an explicit residual.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it is clean. Gate beads I closed today WITH a mutation proof written into the close reason have stayed closed: rf2-4hc9p (3 mutation references), rf2-wns8d (8), rf2-xwa4n (3), rf2-kqxe6.25 (4). Gate beads that got REOPENED carry ZERO mutation references in their notes: rf2-wq17m (0), rf2-as6bg (0). Small n, but the mechanism is obvious once seen.

WHY IT HAPPENS. A gate bead asks "arm this check". The audit asks "does the check CATCH the thing". A close reason that says the job was added, the roster was widened, or the suite is green gives the audit NOTHING TO VERIFY AGAINST — so it reopens and writes the residual itself. A close reason carrying the planted defect, the gate reddening, the restore and the green gives it the verification already done, and it stays closed.

THE RULE: when closing a gate, fixture, census, lane or CI-arming bead, the close reason MUST carry the mutation proof — the specific defect planted, the observed red with counts, the restore, the green. "The job runs" is not "the job catches". If a worker did not supply one, that is a reason to ask for it BEFORE closing, not to close and let the audit find it.

CORROBORATING EVIDENCE FROM TODAY, all of it the same shape: rf2-wns8d proved a shipped deftest was a TAUTOLOGY by mutating the production wrapper and watching the deftest stay GREEN. rf2-4hc9p proved the pre-repair bijection gate was green on all seven planted defects and red on the one prose fixture — exactly inverted. The ci-arming worker found engine_grammar_parity_test.cljc armed on two lanes and matching NEITHER build ns-regexp, so it ran nowhere. In every case the arming was real and the catching was absent, which is precisely the distinction a close reason must record.

SECOND-ORDER POINT WORTH KEEPING: this means the audit reopen rate is partly MY OUTPUT, not just its diligence. Roughly one reopen per merged PR looked like an immovable property of running an audit; a meaningful share of it is gate beads closed on arming rather than on catching. That is fixable from my side.

WHEN A GUARD IS WARRANTED UNDER "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" — the principle that reconciles three decisions I made today (2026-07-26).

The three look contradictory on their face:
  1. rf2-bk7z5 — CLOSED, refusing to validate :role against its documented closed set.
  2. rf2-8o66x — DEFERRED, refusing a performance regression gate.
  3. The empty-export finding — FILED, asking for a row floor in the pre-commit hook.

Two refusals and one request, all under the same posture. The distinguishing principle is not size, cost or priority. It is:

  A GUARD IS WARRANTED WHEN THE FAILURE IS SILENT AND HAS ALREADY HAPPENED. IT IS NOT WARRANTED WHEN THE PROGRAMMER CAN SEE THE FAILURE, OR WHEN THE FAILURE CANNOT OCCUR.

Applied:
  1. :role validation — the failure CANNOT OCCUR. Every producer is in-namespace; no caller can pass an invalid role. Enforcing it adds a failure mode, a message to maintain and a test to keep green, and catches nothing. That is a nag-diagnostic.
  2. The perf gate — the failure would be NOISE, not signal. The no-substrate floor drifted 37% across rounds, larger than most effects being measured, so the gate would red on nothing. And a false red is expensive here precisely because the standing rule is that a failing test on a touched surface is never a flake.
  3. The row floor — the failure IS SILENT AND HAS HAPPENED TWICE, six weeks apart, by the same mechanism. An empty tracker with a CLEAN git status is exactly what a programmer cannot see. That is not distrust; it is the only way the fact becomes visible at all.

SO "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" IS NOT "ASSUME NOTHING GOES WRONG". It is: DO NOT GUARD AGAINST WHAT THE PROGRAMMER CAN ALREADY SEE. A loud crash needs no guard — it is already a signal. A wrong value that renders visibly needs no guard. What needs a guard is the state that looks correct: an empty file with a clean status, a gate green on a defect it was built to catch, a test armed on two lanes and selected by neither.

THE COROLLARY IS THE ONE I HAVE BEEN UNDER-USING: this principle is also a REJECTION criterion with teeth. Most proposed guards fail it, because most proposed failures are either impossible or loud. Ask which of the three cases a proposal is in before pricing it, and the answer usually decides the bead without further analysis.

AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE ERGONOMICS CLAUSE IS A DETECTOR RATHER THAN A BRAKE: a bad diagnostic is the same defect class inverted. The failure IS visible, but it points somewhere useless — an author told to add a key the source already has, or handed a JSON encoding error naming a reified malli class. That is a signal that lies rather than a signal that is missing, and both are worth fixing where a merely-absent convenience is not.

WHERE A FINDING BELONGS WHEN ITS PREMISE IS AN OPEN RULING (2026-07-25, articulated by the R6 worker and worth adopting): a finding whose premise depends on how an OPEN P1 gets ruled belongs on the PR, NOT in the tracker, until that ruling lands.

Concrete case: R6's guide audit found seven canonical recipes omitting an explicit {:sensitive ...} map and recorded the roster on its PR rather than filing beads. rf2-kqxe6.20 then shipped option A — the framework retains its own carrier classification — and the finding DISSOLVED COMPLETELY: those seven recipes had been describing the correct spelling all along; the framework was what needed fixing. Had the roster been beaded, the tracker would now hold a bead instructing people to add boilerplate that spec/012 and the auth how-to explicitly FORBID.

So the test is not 'is this finding real?' but 'is this finding real under every live ruling?'. If the answer depends on a pending decision, park it on the PR where it dies quietly if the ruling moots it, instead of in the tracker where it becomes durable instruction. A dissolved finding is a GOOD outcome to be stated plainly, not salvaged — the R6 worker struck its own roster in the PR comment so nobody would act on it.

WIDE RENAME SWEEPS — check whether the rename silently DISABLES a gate rather than failing it. rf2-lgeron (#6356, 2026-07-18) found the landmine before sweeping 593 alias sites: doc_api_check.clj extracts references for the alias list ["rf" "story"], so renaming story -> rf.story in docs/story/api/** drops ~15 refs; the min-references floor is 20 against a live ~50, so the gate does NOT trip and the Story API page quietly loses reference checking. A green CI would have certified a switched-off check. RULE: before any mechanical rename, grep the GATES for the old token — a checker that counts or allow-lists the thing you are renaming must move in the same PR. Second trap from the same bead: routing/ as an alias is textually indistinguishable from the sanctioned :routing/* late-bind HOOK KEYS (:routing/extra-route-keys, :routing/on-frame-destroyed!), and the same holds for :epoch/* and :schemas/* — a blind sweep corrupts the DI seam grammar. Same family as rf2-bcjpq5 finding :routing/match-url also exists as a conformance CAPABILITY TAG. ALWAYS check for same-spelling distinct meanings before a bulk edit. Third: a sweep spanning surfaces held by live workers cannot be complete-in-one — report the site count and let the mayor sequence it.
